main_damage_causes: Erasure of Pettigrew's arc resolution: the silver hand death — the payoff of Dumbledore's PoA prophecy that saving Pettigrew would matter — is replaced by a neutral Petrification by Dobby, severing the thematic chain of mercy, debt, and redemption that runs across five books and constitutes Pettigrew's entire moral function in the saga.

Absence of psychological backstory: the films never establish young Pettigrew's subordinate, awe-struck relationship with James and Sirius, removing the comprehensible motivation for his betrayal and reducing him from a study in a specific kind of cowardice to a generic functionary.

Compression of the Shrieking Shack and Riddle House confrontations: the extended moral dialectics in PoA and the extended psychological portrait in GoF (Pettigrew's ambivalence, self-assertion, and Voldemort's contempt) are heavily truncated, stripping Pettigrew of the interiority that makes him one of the saga's most thematically significant secondary characters.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Shrieking Shack confrontation: Pettigrew's confession compressed and reordered
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 91–170) establishes an extended, psychologically rich confrontation in which Pettigrew grovels to each person in turn, offers multiple self-justifications ('He was taking over everywhere!', 'He would have killed me, Sirius!'), is systematically exposed by Black and Lupin through evidence and argument, admits guilt by bursting into tears, and reveals cowardice as a deep character trait across many beats. His moral culpability is laid out in detail: he was a spy for a year before the Potters died, he chose safety over loyalty, and Black articulates exactly why: 'You always liked big friends who'd look after you.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scene 7) compresses Pettigrew's confession to a few lines: 'I didn't mean to! The Dark Lord, you have no idea the weapons he possesses! Ask yourself what you would have done, Sirius. What would you have done!' The extended groveling, the multiple rounds of self-justification, the systematic dismantling of his excuses by Lupin and Black, and the tearful breakdown are all absent or severely truncated. The film moves quickly past his exposure to the decision about his fate.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's confrontation is the definitive characterization of Pettigrew as a specific type of coward — not simply evil, but a calculating opportunist who chose the winning side. The film's compression strips away the layers of self-justification and the systematic moral indictment delivered by Black ('What was there to be gained by fighting? Only innocent lives, Peter!'). This diminishes the ideological weight of the scene and reduces Pettigrew from a complex study in cowardice to a simple villain making a rushed excuse.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Shrieking Shack: Black's line 'Died! Died rather than betray my friends!' replaces extended dialectic
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 156–163) shows Black and Pettigrew engaged in a back-and-forth moral argument: Pettigrew cries 'He would have killed me, Sirius!'; Black responds 'THEN YOU SHOULD HAVE DIED! DIED RATHER THAN BETRAY YOUR FRIENDS, AS WE WOULD HAVE DONE FOR YOU!' This exchange is the moral climax of Pettigrew's exposure, establishing that the Marauders held a code of loyalty unto death, and that Pettigrew knew and violated it consciously.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scene 7) has Sirius deliver a collapsed version: 'Died! Died rather than betray my friends! And you should have realized, Peter, if Voldemort didn't kill you...' followed immediately by Lupin completing '...we would.' The exchange is present but the preceding back-and-forth — Pettigrew's escalating self-justifications and Sirius's point-by-point rebuttals — is absent, making Black's line feel like a declaration rather than the conclusion of a moral argument.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Pettigrew's cowardice is most damaging to the reader/viewer when it is shown to be a conscious, reasoned choice rather than simple weakness. The book makes him argue for his survival; the film denies him enough rope to fully hang himself, slightly reducing the moral clarity of his betrayal and the specific nature of his character flaw.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Pettigrew's groveling to Ron, Hermione, and Harry truncated
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 135–155) shows Pettigrew performing a full circuit of groveling: falling to his knees when Harry nods, shuffling toward Sirius ('your friend... you wouldn't—'), being kicked away, turning to Lupin, writhing imploringly, turning to Ron ('Haven't I been a good friend... a good pet?'), being repulsed, seizing Hermione's robes ('Sweet girl... clever girl... you — you won't let them...'), then finally crawling toward Harry and invoking James Potter ('James would have understood, Harry... he would have shown me mercy'). Each refusal deepens his humiliation and isolation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scene 7) shows Pettigrew appealing to Ron ('Haven't I been a good friend? A good pet?') and Hermione ('Sweet girl. Clever girl. Surely you won't let them...') in brief succession, but the full circuit — the kicking away by Black, the writhing before Lupin, and crucially the invocation of James Potter to Harry — is absent or significantly compressed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The groveling circuit in the book is essential to showing that Pettigrew has no genuine relationships — only transactional ones. Each person's revulsion confirms his isolation. The invocation of James to Harry is particularly important because it shows Pettigrew is willing to instrumentalize Harry's grief over his dead father, which is his most contemptible act in the scene. Losing this detail softens the full portrait of his moral bankruptcy.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Harry's reasoning for sparing Pettigrew simplified
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scene 169) shows Harry articulating a specific moral position: 'I'm not doing this for you. I'm doing it because — I don't reckon my dad would've wanted them to become killers — just for you.' This is a considered, principled act that simultaneously honors James, rejects Pettigrew's attempt to invoke James ('he would have shown me mercy'), and establishes Harry's moral identity as distinct from revenge.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scene 7) has Harry say: 'I don't reckon my father'd want his best friends to become killers for a worthless piece of vermin like Pettigrew. Besides: Dead, the truth dies with him. Alive... you're free.' The film adds a practical, instrumental reason (Sirius needs Pettigrew alive to be freed) that is not present in the book at this moment and dilutes the purely moral character of Harry's decision.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Harry's mercy is a purely moral act — he gains nothing from it and knows Pettigrew will likely escape. The film partially converts it into a strategic choice (keep him alive to free Sirius), which undermines the theme Dumbledore later develops (scenes 244–248): that saving Pettigrew creates a bond of debt that will matter later. Harry's act needs to be gratuitous mercy to carry that thematic weight, and the film's added pragmatic motive weakens it.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Pettigrew's escape: loss of the Expelliarmus beat and Harry's active role
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 200–202) shows Harry casting 'Expelliarmus' at Pettigrew when he dives for Lupin's dropped wand, actively preventing Pettigrew from arming himself — but too late, as Pettigrew has already transformed. Harry is an active agent in the escape sequence, not merely a bystander.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scene 8) shows Harry cast 'Expelliarmus' and Lupin's wand fly from Pettigrew's hand, after which Pettigrew 'freezes... then slowly turns. Face blank, eyes closed, he... GRINS HIDEOUSLY. Transforms.' The film retains Harry casting the spell, which is faithful, but the transformation sequence is rendered as Pettigrew's own volition (grinning hideously before transforming) rather than the desperate last-second escape of the book, slightly altering the tone of inevitability.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor tonal shift. The book's escape feels desperate and lucky for Pettigrew; the film's version (grinning hideously) makes it feel more calculated and sinister, which is a small but genuine departure from the book's characterization of Pettigrew as a creature of instinct and panic rather than cool calculation.

damaging_scenes.scene: GoF Film - Riddle House opening: Pettigrew's internal conflict and dialogue with Voldemort drastically cut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 258–319) establishes Pettigrew in an extended scene at the Riddle House in which he: pushes for using a different wizard instead of Harry ('It could be done without Harry Potter, My Lord'); is accused by Voldemort of wanting to desert him; flinches at the mention of Voldemort's name; is told his 'devotion is nothing more than cowardice'; argues back with a 'sulky edge' ('I found you... I was the one who found you. I brought you Bertha Jorkins'); and shows genuine ambivalence about his role. This is the fullest portrait of Pettigrew's psychology in the saga: simultaneously subservient, self-pitying, occasionally defiant, and trapped.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scene 12) reduces the Riddle House to a brief exchange: Voldemort accuses Wormtail of wanting to proceed without the boy ('if we were to do it without the boy...'), Voldemort insists ('The boy is everything!'), and Wormtail is essentially a silent functionary thereafter. None of the extended psychological back-and-forth, Pettigrew's attempt to bargain for a substitute, his sulky assertion of his own value, or Voldemort's characterization of his devotion as cowardice appears.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Riddle House dialogue is the primary establishment of Pettigrew's ongoing psychological state post-PoA: trapped, ambivalent, occasionally self-assertive, and genuinely afraid of both his master and his former friends. The film reduces him to a near-mute servant. This matters because the GoF book sequence seeds everything — his reluctance, his tenuous sense of self-worth, the silver hand's later significance. Without it, Pettigrew is simply 'Voldemort's helper' with no interiority.

damaging_scenes.scene: GoF Film - Graveyard resurrection: Pettigrew's emotional state and agency compressed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 365–431) portrays Pettigrew performing the resurrection ritual with shaking hands, 'petrified sobs,' explicit revulsion at lowering the Voldemort-creature into the cauldron ('the look of revulsion on Wormtail's weak, pale face'), whimpering as he cuts off his hand, and collapsing afterward 'cradling the bleeding stump of his arm, gasping and sobbing.' After the resurrection he is thrown against the headstone by Voldemort, told 'you returned to me not out of loyalty, but out of fear,' and given the silver hand as a conditional reward.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scene 15) retains the three-part incantation and self-mutilation, but the extended psychological texture — the revulsion at the creature, the petrified sobbing, the collapsing and cradling — is rendered through action description rather than dialogue and is significantly compressed. The film does retain 'Out of fear, not loyalty' and the silver hand reward. The core beats survive but the granular emotional performance detail from the book is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's resurrection sequence is important for showing that Pettigrew is not a true believer — he is visibly revolted by his master's form, performs the ritual in terror, and is treated contemptuously even after succeeding. The film preserves the plot but loses the psychological undercurrent that distinguishes Pettigrew from loyal Death Eaters. This is a moderate loss of characterization nuance.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Spinner's End: Pettigrew reduced to a silent domestic servant
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 511–516) establishes Pettigrew at Spinner's End asserting himself against Snape: 'I am not your servant!'; 'To assist, yes — but not to make you drinks and — and clean your house!'; 'I can speak to him myself if I want to!' He is humiliated but combative, and the scene shows his ambiguous status — neither fully trusted by Voldemort nor content in his subordinate role — and his resentment of Snape specifically.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scenes 17–19) shows Wormtail answering the door, leading the sisters down the hallway, and being dismissed by Snape with 'Run along, Wormtail' — with no dialogue from Pettigrew and no scene of him asserting himself or arguing back. He is a functionary who opens a door and disappears.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Spinner's End argument is one of only two scenes in the later books where Pettigrew shows any self-assertion or resentment. Reducing him to a silent doorman eliminates the last trace of his personality beyond pure servility, flattening a character who in the books retains a querulous, self-pitying voice even in submission. It also removes the specific dynamic with Snape that illustrates Pettigrew's degraded status in the Death Eater hierarchy.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Film - Malfoy Manor cellar: Pettigrew's death by silver hand absent/off-screen
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 537–546) shows Pettigrew's silver hand turning against him in the moment he hesitates to strangle Harry — 'the tiny, merciful impulse it had betrayed' — and slowly strangling him to death as Harry and Ron try futilely to pull the fingers free. This is the fulfillment of Dumbledore's prophecy in PoA that saving Pettigrew would matter, and it is the culmination of Pettigrew's entire arc: he dies because of one unconscious moment of mercy, and the silver hand — Voldemort's gift — kills him for it.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scene 25) shows Wormtail being Petrified by Dobby ('Harry and Ron stiffen, then watch Wormtail fall forward, stiff as a board'), with Dobby producing Wormtail's wand and asking 'Who gets his wand?' There is no silver hand turning on Pettigrew, no strangling, no moment of mercy, no death on screen. Pettigrew is simply incapacitated and thereafter absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most structurally damaging single change to Pettigrew's portrayal. His death by silver hand is the payoff of a narrative thread established in PoA: Harry spares him, Dumbledore tells Harry it was 'magic at its deepest,' and the debt comes due in DH when Pettigrew's hand kills him for showing Harry mercy. The film replaces this with a neutral Petrification by Dobby. The thematic chain — mercy creates debt, debt manifests, Pettigrew is redeemed and destroyed by the same impulse — is completely severed. This is a saga-level loss because it erases one of the saga's explicit demonstrations of how love and mercy function as magic, and it removes Pettigrew's only moment of moral agency. Dumbledore's speech in PoA (book scenes 244–248) is rendered thematically inert by this change.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Film - No acknowledgment of Pettigrew's death and its meaning
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scene 558) shows Harry reflecting: 'And he thought of Wormtail, dead because of one small unconscious impulse of mercy... Dumbledore had foreseen that... How much more had he known?' This is an explicit authorial statement about the meaning of Pettigrew's death within the saga's moral framework.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus contains no equivalent reflection. Pettigrew simply disappears from the narrative after being Petrified. There is no acknowledgment of his death, no callback to PoA, and no thematic closure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The absence of Harry's reflection is a direct consequence of the changed death scene. Even if the death had been shown differently, the loss of this moment means the audience has no way to understand that Pettigrew's fate was foreseen and meaningful within the saga's moral logic. Combined with the changed death scene, this absence completes the erasure of Pettigrew's arc resolution.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Background of the Marauders: Pettigrew's role as dependent, awe-struck follower not established
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 487–509) shows the young Pettigrew at Hogwarts: anxiously chewing fingernails during exams, staring at James 'in awe,' gasping and applauding James's Snitch catches, being teased by Sirius ('before Wormtail wets himself with excitement'), watching 'hungrily' as Snape is tormented, and laughing shrilly. Lupin's account (scenes 57–64) establishes that 'Peter needed all the help he could get from James and Sirius' for the Animagus transformation, and McGonagall notes he was 'Never quite in their league, talent-wise.' The composite portrait is of a hanger-on who hero-worshipped James and Sirius, was kept around partly out of pity, and whose dependence made him susceptible to Voldemort's offer of a more powerful patron.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus contains no flashback or scene establishing young Pettigrew's relationship dynamic with the Marauders. Lupin's exposition in Scene 7 states only that 'He was at school with us. We thought he was a friend.' The psychological foundation explaining why Pettigrew was vulnerable to betrayal — his subordinate status, his need for powerful protectors — is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's backstory is essential to making Pettigrew's betrayal comprehensible rather than arbitrary. Sirius's accusation — 'You always liked big friends who'd look after you... It must have been the finest moment of your miserable life, telling Voldemort you could hand him the Potters' — lands with full force because we understand how long Pettigrew had played second fiddle. Without this context, his betrayal seems like generic villainy. The film's Pettigrew has no comprehensible psychology, only a function.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Marauder's Map scene: Pettigrew's dot on the map not used to seed awareness of his psychology
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (scenes 30–35) establishes that the Map insults Snape as 'Mr. Wormtail,' and Lupin's reaction to hearing Harry has seen 'Peter Pettigrew' on the map is an 'odd, closed expression' — a subtle signal that Lupin knows Pettigrew is alive. The map is also the mechanism by which Lupin finally confirms Pettigrew's survival.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus (Scenes 3–6) retains Harry seeing 'Peter Pettigrew' on the map and telling Lupin, who 'hesitates ever-so-slightly, then returns to his papers.' This is reasonably faithful. The map insult scene is also present. This is not a major source of damage.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor: the film handles this adequately. Lupin's hesitation is present. The damage here is negligible and scored low accordingly.
